drafted_from: tool:trade-a-tool-servers-sign-in-code-for-its-tokens's own row (its words and input schema); the command line's connect runs it when you come back from a tool server's sign-in page, and a person does not ask for it by hand
start_here: You do not run this yourself: `{cli} connect ADDRESS` runs it when you come back from a remote tool server's sign-in page, with the code that page handed back. It trades the code at the server's own token address and keeps the access token (reaching only the server), the refresh token (reaching only the token address), the token address and the client id in your vault as the fields of the server's connection (service_connection:tool-server:<the server's host>). Then any AI calls the server's tools by its address: tools:list or tools:run with {"address": ADDRESS}.
no_lists_because: It keeps the tokens in your vault, not in a list.
instructions: 1. Ask your AI to connect the tool server at its address; it runs `{cli} connect ADDRESS`.
2. Open the sign-in address it gives you and sign in on the server's own page.
3. This tool then trades the code for tokens and keeps them in your vault; the server's tools answer at once by its address.

worked_examples.title: The code from one sign-in
worked_examples.ask: Connect the tool server at https://tools.example.com/mcp (it asks for a sign-in)
worked_examples.given: The code the server's sign-in page handed back, the callback address the sign-in was started with, the PKCE verifier kept for it and the client id it registered.
worked_examples.hands_back: It answered {"token_type":"bearer"} with each token replaced by the held word; the tokens, the token address and the client id are now held in your vault under the connection service_connection:tool-server:tools.example.com.
